title: Labs & Imaging
summary: How to read a lab report and a radiology study the way a clinician does: what each number means, what makes it wrong, which ones kill you today, and which test to order in the first place.

lessons.title: How to read a lab report
lessons.body:
## A number is meaningless without its range

A **reference range** is not a definition of health. It is the middle `95%` of results from a group of people the lab decided were normal. That means `1 in 20` perfectly healthy people falls outside the range on any given test, by arithmetic alone.

Ranges differ between hospitals because analyzers, reagents, and reference populations differ. Read the range printed next to the value on that report, not the one you memorized. Units matter for the same reason: creatinine is `mg/dL` in the United States and `micromol/L` in most of the world, and the numbers look nothing alike.

## Critical values get a phone call

A **critical value** (old slang: panic value) is a result so far off that it threatens life in hours. The lab does not put it in the chart and move on. A technologist telephones a licensed provider, the provider repeats the value back, and the read-back is documented with the time and both names.

Typical critical thresholds, which vary by lab: potassium below `2.8` or above `6.2 mEq/L`, sodium below `120` or above `160 mEq/L`, glucose below `50` or above `450 mg/dL`, calcium below `6.5` or above `13 mg/dL`, platelets below `20,000`, hemoglobin below `7 g/dL`, INR above `5.0`, lactate above `4 mmol/L`, and any positive blood culture.

## Delta checks and the disbelief rule

A **delta check** compares a result to that patient's own previous one. A creatinine that goes `0.9` to `3.4 mg/dL` in twelve hours trips it. Either the kidney failed or the specimen is not this patient's blood.

> **Key:** When a number does not match the patient in front of you, suspect the specimen before you suspect the physiology. Recollect first, treat second.

## What goes wrong in the tube

| Problem | What it is | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Hemolyzed | Red cells burst in the tube | Potassium, LDH, AST falsely high. The number one cause of fake hyperkalemia |
| Clotted | Sample clotted before analysis | CBC unusable, platelets falsely low |
| QNS | Quantity not sufficient, tube underfilled | Blue-top coags need a full tube for the `9:1` blood-to-citrate ratio. Underfilled means falsely long PT and INR |
| Lipemic | Milky fat in the serum | Blocks optical reading, causes pseudohyponatremia |
| IV contamination | Drawn above a running line | Glucose `600` with diluted everything else |

Order of draw exists for the same reason: blue, then gold or red, then green, then lavender, then gray. Carryover of lavender-top EDTA into a chemistry tube falsely raises potassium and falsely lowers calcium.

## Point of care versus the central lab

A point-of-care (POC) analyzer at the bedside returns a chemistry or blood gas in `2` to `10` minutes on a few drops. The central lab needs roughly `30` to `60` minutes for routine chemistry and longer for send-outs. POC trades precision for speed, and POC glucose meters are least accurate at the extremes and in shocked, poorly perfused patients. Confirm a critical POC value with a lab draw.

## What a result actually tells you

**Sensitivity** is how well a test catches disease when it is there. **Specificity** is how well it stays quiet when disease is absent. Two phrases carry the logic:

- **SnNout:** a highly **S**e**n**sitive test, when **N**egative, rules the disease **out**.
- **SpPin:** a highly **Sp**ecific test, when **P**ositive, rules the disease **in**.

> **Trap:** Both only work if you asked a sensible question first. A test ordered on a patient with near-zero pretest probability produces mostly false positives, and every false positive buys a scan, a consult, and a needle.
keyPoints: A reference range is the middle 95% of a normal group, so 1 in 20 healthy people is out of range by definition
Critical values require a phone call to a licensed provider with a documented read-back
Hemolysis fakes hyperkalemia, an underfilled blue top fakes a long INR, and a line draw fakes everything
Delta check logic: a number that does not match the patient is a specimen problem until proven otherwise
SnNout and SpPin: sensitive tests rule out when negative, specific tests rule in when positive

checks.q: A potassium of 6.4 mEq/L comes back on a well-appearing outpatient with a normal ECG. The specimen is flagged hemolyzed. What is the next step?
choices: Redraw the specimen with a clean, atraumatic stick
Report the value as a true critical result and admit
checks.why: Hemolysis spills potassium out of red cells inside the tube and is the most common cause of falsely high potassium. A well patient with a normal ECG and a hemolyzed sample gets a redraw, not treatment.

checks.q: A blue-top coagulation tube is filled only halfway. What happens to the result?
choices: The PT and INR are falsely prolonged
The PT and INR are falsely shortened
The platelet count is falsely low
checks.why: Citrate anticoagulant is pre-measured for a full tube at a 9:1 blood-to-citrate ratio. Less blood means relatively more citrate, which binds more calcium and falsely prolongs clotting times. Platelets come from the lavender top, not the blue.

checks.q: Which phrase describes why a negative D-dimer is useful in a low-risk patient?
choices: SpPin, because it is highly specific
SnNout, because it is highly sensitive
checks.why: D-dimer is sensitive but not specific. A negative result on a sensitive test rules the disease out, which is SnNout. It is positive in too many conditions to rule anything in, so SpPin does not apply.

lessons.title: The CBC, line by line
lessons.body:
## One lavender tube, three cell lines

The complete blood count (CBC) is drawn in a lavender-top EDTA tube and run through a counter that sizes and sorts every cell it sees. It reports three independent stories: the white cells (the immune system), the red cells (oxygen carrying), and the platelets (clotting).

## White cells and the differential

Normal white blood cell count (WBC) is `4,500` to `11,000` per microliter. Above `11,000` is **leukocytosis**: infection, but also steroids, stress, trauma, seizures, and leukemia. Below `4,500` is **leukopenia**: viral illness, chemotherapy, marrow failure, and overwhelming sepsis that consumes cells faster than the marrow makes them.

The **differential** splits that total into five cell types, in order of abundance:

| Cell | Percent | Goes up with |
|---|---|---|
| Neutrophils | `40-70%` | Bacterial infection, acute inflammation, steroids |
| Lymphocytes | `20-40%` | Viral infection, pertussis |
| Monocytes | `2-8%` | Chronic infection, tuberculosis |
| Eosinophils | `1-4%` | Allergy, asthma, parasites, drug reaction |
| Basophils | `0-1%` | Rarely anything but chronic myeloid leukemia |

Neutrophils live about `7` hours in blood. When bacteria consume them, the marrow ships out immature forms called **bands**. Seeing them is a **left shift**. Bands above `10%` (bandemia) points at serious bacterial infection.

> **Trap:** Bandemia can appear with a totally normal total WBC. A normal white count does not exclude sepsis, and neither does a normal temperature.

## The ANC, the number that decides isolation

The absolute neutrophil count (ANC) is the real infection-fighting force:

`ANC = WBC x (% segs + % bands) / 100`

A WBC of `2,000` with `30%` segs and `5%` bands gives `2,000 x 0.35 = 700`.

Below `1,500` is neutropenia, below `1,000` is moderate, below `500` is severe. Fever plus an ANC below `500` is **febrile neutropenia**, an emergency: cultures then broad-spectrum antibiotics within `60` minutes, and no rectal temperatures or rectal exams because the mucosa is a doorway for gut bacteria.

## Red cells

Hemoglobin (Hgb) is `13.5` to `17.5 g/dL` in men and `12.0` to `15.5 g/dL` in women. Hematocrit (Hct) is the percentage of blood volume that is red cells, and it runs about three times the hemoglobin. That is the **rule of 3**: Hgb `10` means Hct near `30`. If they do not track, question the sample.

Transfusion is restrictive because stored blood carries risk. Threshold `7 g/dL` for most stable hospitalized patients, `8 g/dL` for cardiac surgery, active coronary syndrome, and hip or knee surgery. One unit of packed red cells raises hemoglobin about `1 g/dL` and hematocrit about `3%`.

> **Key:** In acute hemorrhage the hemoglobin is normal at first. You are losing whole blood, so the concentration does not fall until fluid shifts in or you give crystalloid. A normal Hgb never rules out active bleeding.

Mean corpuscular volume (MCV), normal `80` to `100 fL`, sorts anemia into three buckets: small cells (under `80`) mean iron deficiency, thalassemia, chronic disease, or lead; normal-sized cells mean acute blood loss, hemolysis, or kidney disease; large cells (over `100`) mean B12 or folate deficiency, alcohol, liver disease, or hypothyroidism.

## Platelets

Normal is `150,000` to `400,000` per microliter. The thresholds worth memorizing: below `50,000` cancel elective procedures and expect bleeding with trauma, below `20,000` transfuse if febrile or bleeding, below `10,000` transfuse prophylactically because spontaneous bleeding, including intracranial, becomes real.
keyPoints: ANC = WBC x (segs + bands) / 100; below 500 with fever is an antibiotics-within-60-minutes emergency
Left shift means bands, and bandemia can occur with a normal total WBC
Hct is roughly 3x Hgb; transfuse at 7 g/dL, or 8 g/dL for cardiac and orthopedic patients
MCV sorts anemia: under 80 iron and thalassemia, 80-100 blood loss and hemolysis, over 100 B12 folate and alcohol
Platelet thresholds: 50,000 for procedures, 20,000 with fever or bleeding, 10,000 for spontaneous bleeding

checks.q: A chemotherapy patient has a WBC of 1,200 with 35% segs and 5% bands, and a temperature of 38.6 C. What is the ANC and what does it demand?
choices: ANC 480, observe and repeat the CBC in the morning
checks.why: 1,200 x (35 + 5) / 100 = 480, well under 500. Fever plus severe neutropenia is febrile neutropenia, which requires cultures and broad-spectrum antibiotics within one hour, plus no rectal temperatures or exams.

checks.q: A 68-year-old man has Hgb 9.1 g/dL and MCV 71 fL. Which cause is most likely and what should be pursued?
choices: Iron deficiency from gastrointestinal blood loss, pursue endoscopy
Marrow failure, order a biopsy first
checks.why: An MCV of 71 is microcytic, and the commonest microcytic anemia in an adult is iron deficiency. In an older man that means occult gastrointestinal blood loss until proven otherwise. B12 deficiency raises the MCV above 100; hemolysis is usually normocytic.

checks.q: A trauma patient 20 minutes after a gunshot wound has a hemoglobin of 14.2 g/dL. What does that tell you?
choices: Very little, because acute whole blood loss does not lower the concentration yet
checks.why: Whole blood loss removes plasma and cells in the same ratio, so the measured concentration stays normal until fluid shifts in or crystalloid is given. Early hemoglobin cannot exclude hemorrhage; the exam, vitals, and FAST do.

lessons.title: The basic metabolic panel and the anion gap
lessons.body:
## Eight numbers that describe the internal ocean

The basic metabolic panel (BMP) is drawn in a green or gold top and tells you about water, salt, acid, kidney, and sugar. It is the single most ordered panel in the emergency department because it screens all of those at once.

| Test | Range | High suggests | Low suggests |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sodium | `135-145 mEq/L` | Dehydration, diabetes insipidus | SIADH, heart failure, thiazides, beer potomania |
| Potassium | `3.5-5.0 mEq/L` | Kidney failure, acidosis, crush injury, ACE inhibitors | Vomiting, diarrhea, loop diuretics, insulin |
| Chloride | `98-107 mEq/L` | Saline loading, renal tubular acidosis | Vomiting, gastric suction |
| CO2 (bicarbonate) | `22-28 mEq/L` | Vomiting, respiratory compensation | Metabolic acidosis, the first clue to sepsis or DKA |
| BUN | `7-20 mg/dL` | Dehydration, GI bleed, kidney failure | Liver failure, malnutrition |
| Creatinine | `0.6-1.2 mg/dL` | Kidney injury | Low muscle mass |
| Glucose | `70-99 mg/dL` fasting | Diabetes, stress, steroids | Insulin, sepsis, liver failure, alcohol |
| Calcium | `8.5-10.5 mg/dL` | Malignancy, hyperparathyroidism | Pancreatitis, transfusion, renal failure |

## Sodium is a water problem, not a salt problem

Sodium concentration tells you how much water the salt is dissolved in. A sodium of `118 mEq/L` with a seizure is treated with hypertonic `3%` saline, roughly `100 mL` over `10` minutes, repeated to stop the seizing. After that, correction must not exceed about `8 mEq/L` in `24` hours, because pulling water out of brain cells too fast causes osmotic demyelination.

## Potassium talks to the heart

Potassium sets the resting membrane potential, so it shows up on the ECG before it shows up in symptoms. Above `6.0 mEq/L` expect peaked T waves; higher, the QRS widens toward a sine wave. Treatment order: calcium gluconate `1 g IV` to stabilize the membrane (it does not lower potassium), then insulin `10 units` with `25 g` dextrose and albuterol to drive potassium into cells, then something that removes it.

## BUN, creatinine, and the ratio

Creatinine comes from muscle at a steady rate and is filtered, so it tracks kidney function. BUN is urea from protein breakdown, and the kidney reabsorbs it along with sodium and water when the body is dry.

> **Key:** A `BUN:creatinine ratio above 20:1` means the kidney is holding on to water. That is pre-renal: dehydration, hemorrhage, heart failure, or a gastrointestinal bleed feeding a protein load into the gut.

## Calcium needs its albumin

Half of calcium rides on albumin, and the analyzer reports total calcium. In a malnourished or cirrhotic patient with a low albumin, the total looks low while the active ionized fraction is fine.

`Corrected calcium = measured calcium + 0.8 x (4.0 - albumin)`

## The anion gap

`Anion gap = Na - (Cl + HCO3)`, normal `8` to `12 mEq/L`. It measures unmeasured anions. When an acid is added to the blood, bicarbonate is consumed neutralizing it and the acid's anion takes its place, so the gap widens.

**MUDPILES** names the causes: **M**ethanol, **U**remia, **D**iabetic ketoacidosis, **P**ropylene glycol, **I**ron or **I**soniazid, **L**actate, **E**thylene glycol, **S**alicylates.

## The chemistries the BMP does not show

Magnesium `1.7-2.2 mg/dL`, phosphate `2.5-4.5 mg/dL`, uric acid `3.5-7.2 mg/dL`. Low magnesium makes potassium impossible to replace and prolongs the QT. HbA1c reflects three months of glucose: `5.7-6.4%` is prediabetes and `6.5%` or higher is diabetes. TSH `0.4-4.0 mU/L` with free T4 `0.8-1.8 ng/dL`: high TSH with low free T4 is primary hypothyroidism, low TSH with high free T4 is hyperthyroidism.
keyPoints: Anion gap = Na - (Cl + HCO3), normal 8-12; a wide gap means MUDPILES
A low bicarbonate on a routine BMP is often the first objective sign of sepsis or DKA
BUN:creatinine above 20:1 means pre-renal: dehydration, hemorrhage, or a GI bleed
Corrected calcium = measured + 0.8 x (4.0 - albumin)
Hyperkalemia treatment order: calcium to protect the heart, insulin with dextrose and albuterol to shift, then remove

checks.q: Na 132, Cl 94, HCO3 10, glucose 480. What is the anion gap and the likely diagnosis?
checks.why: 132 - (94 + 10) = 28, well above the normal 8-12. A wide gap with a glucose of 480 is DKA, where ketoacids consume bicarbonate. Vomiting causes a high bicarbonate, not a gap.

checks.q: An 80-year-old with vomiting for three days has BUN 62 and creatinine 1.3 mg/dL. What does the ratio indicate?
choices: Intrinsic kidney damage from acute tubular necrosis
checks.why: The ratio is about 48:1, far above 20:1. The kidney reabsorbs urea along with sodium and water when volume depleted, so BUN rises out of proportion to creatinine. Acute tubular necrosis gives a ratio closer to 10:1 to 15:1.

checks.q: Total calcium is 7.4 mg/dL and albumin is 2.0 g/dL. What is the corrected calcium?
checks.why: Corrected = 7.4 + 0.8 x (4.0 - 2.0) = 7.4 + 1.6 = 9.0 mg/dL, inside the 8.5-10.5 range. The low total reflects low carrier protein, not low active calcium.

lessons.title: Liver, pancreas, and the rest of the CMP
lessons.body:
## The CMP is the BMP plus the liver

A comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP) adds seven tests to the BMP: AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase, total bilirubin, direct bilirubin, albumin, and total protein. Two of them are enzymes leaking out of injured cells, two are proteins the liver makes, and the rest describe the plumbing.

| Test | Range | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| AST | `10-40 U/L` | Inside hepatocytes, also heart and muscle |
| ALT | `7-56 U/L` | Almost only liver, so more specific |
| Alkaline phosphatase | `44-147 U/L` | Bile ducts and bone |
| Total bilirubin | `0.1-1.2 mg/dL` | Heme breakdown product |
| Direct bilirubin | `0.0-0.3 mg/dL` | The conjugated, water-soluble fraction |
| Albumin | `3.5-5.0 g/dL` | Liver synthetic function, slow marker |
| Total protein | `6.0-8.3 g/dL` | Albumin plus globulins |

## Two patterns, and you must name one

**Hepatocellular** injury means cells are dying and spilling enzymes: AST and ALT rise far out of proportion to alkaline phosphatase. **Cholestatic** injury means bile cannot get out: alkaline phosphatase and direct bilirubin lead, with only modest transaminase rise. Gallstones, tumors, and drug-induced cholestasis live here.

If alkaline phosphatase is high, a GGT sorts the source. High GGT means liver or bile duct. Normal GGT with high alkaline phosphatase means bone: Paget disease, metastases, or a growing adolescent.

## Three signatures worth recognizing on sight

- **Alcohol:** `AST:ALT ratio above 2:1`, with both usually under `300 U/L`. Remember it as "you toAST with alcohol."
- **Acetaminophen:** transaminases in the thousands, sometimes above `5,000 U/L`, with a bilirubin that is still nearly normal early, and an INR that starts climbing.
- **Shock liver (ischemic hepatitis):** a massive spike into the thousands within `24` hours of hypotension, an LDH that rises with it, then a rapid fall over days once perfusion returns.

Viral hepatitis and fatty liver usually run `ALT above AST`, in the hundreds.

> **Trap:** AST is also in skeletal muscle and heart. An isolated AST elevation after a hard workout, a seizure, or rhabdomyolysis is muscle, not liver. Check a CK before you blame the liver.

## Bilirubin tells you where the problem is

Unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin rises when heme is broken down faster than the liver can conjugate it, or when conjugation is lazy: hemolysis and Gilbert syndrome. Conjugated (direct) bilirubin rises when the liver conjugated it fine but it cannot leave: stones, strictures, tumors, and intrahepatic cholestasis. Direct hyperbilirubinemia is the one that turns urine dark.

## Albumin is a slow marker, INR is the fast one

Albumin has a half-life near `20` days, so it drops in chronic liver disease, malnutrition, nephrotic syndrome, and chronic inflammation, but stays normal in acute hepatitis. Clotting factors have half-lives of hours, so in acute liver failure the **INR is the synthetic function test that moves first**, which is why it sits inside the liver failure criteria.

## Pancreas: lipase, and the rule of three

Lipase is the pancreatic test that matters. A lipase at or above `3x` the upper limit of normal, in a patient with typical epigastric pain radiating to the back, establishes acute pancreatitis without imaging. Lipase stays elevated `8` to `14` days; amylase clears in `3` to `5` days and is far less specific, since parotitis, bowel ischemia, and ectopic pregnancy raise it too.

> **Key:** The height of the lipase does not predict severity. A lipase of `4,000` is not worse than `900`. Severity comes from the vitals, the calcium, the BUN, and the organ failures.

Ammonia runs `15-45 micromol/L`. It is associated with hepatic encephalopathy, but the level correlates poorly with mental status, so treat the patient and not the number.
keyPoints: Hepatocellular means AST and ALT lead; cholestatic means alkaline phosphatase and direct bilirubin lead
AST:ALT above 2:1 is alcohol; transaminases above 1,000 mean acetaminophen, ischemia, or viral hepatitis
Indirect bilirubin points to hemolysis or Gilbert; direct bilirubin points to obstruction
INR is the fast synthetic marker in acute liver failure; albumin is the slow, chronic one
Lipase at 3x the upper limit with typical pain diagnoses pancreatitis, and the height does not predict severity

checks.q: A patient found down after a long hypotensive episode has AST 4,800, ALT 3,900, LDH 2,100, bilirubin 1.4. Two days later they are down to 900. What is this?
checks.why: A huge transaminase spike with a high LDH after hypotension that falls rapidly is shock liver. Viral hepatitis rises and falls over weeks. Obstruction leads with alkaline phosphatase and direct bilirubin. Alcoholic hepatitis rarely exceeds 300 and keeps AST above ALT at a 2:1 ratio.

checks.q: Alkaline phosphatase is 340 U/L with normal transaminases, normal bilirubin, and a normal GGT. Where is the problem?
checks.why: Alkaline phosphatase comes from bile ducts and bone. A normal GGT excludes a hepatobiliary source, pointing at bone: Paget disease, metastases, healing fracture, or normal adolescent growth.

checks.q: Which single value best reflects acute liver synthetic failure within hours?
checks.why: Clotting factors made by the liver have half-lives measured in hours, so the INR rises quickly in acute failure. Albumin has a roughly 20-day half-life and stays normal early. Alkaline phosphatase measures cholestasis, not synthesis.

lessons.title: Cardiac markers: troponin, BNP, and CK
lessons.body:
## Troponin is a structural protein, not a diagnosis

Troponin I and T are proteins that sit on the contractile machinery of heart muscle. They are not in the blood in any meaningful amount unless myocytes are dying or badly stressed. High-sensitivity assays (hs-troponin, reported in `ng/L`) detect concentrations roughly ten times lower than the older ones, which is why almost everyone now has a measurable level.

The upper reference limit is the `99th percentile` of a healthy population and is **sex-specific**, commonly around `34 ng/L` for men and `16 ng/L` for women on a typical assay. The exact numbers vary by assay, so read the lab's own cutoffs.

## The delta is the test, not the single value

Because everyone has a number, the algorithm depends on change over time. A `0/1-hour` or `0/2-hour` protocol draws a baseline and repeats it:

- **Rule out:** a very low initial value (often under `5 ng/L`) with symptoms for more than `3` hours, or a low baseline with a tiny delta over the interval.
- **Rule in:** a high baseline, or a delta above the assay's threshold. A rising and falling pattern means acute injury.
- **Observe:** everything in between gets a third troponin and more thought.

> **Key:** A single elevated troponin says myocardial injury. It does not say myocardial infarction, and it never says which artery. The story, the ECG, and the trend say that.

## Non-ACS causes of a positive troponin

Type 1 myocardial infarction is plaque rupture with thrombus. **Type 2** is supply and demand mismatch with no plaque event: sepsis, tachyarrhythmia, severe anemia, hypotension, hypertensive crisis. Then there is injury without infarction at all:

- Pulmonary embolism, through right ventricular strain
- Chronic kidney disease, through reduced clearance, giving a stably elevated baseline
- Myocarditis, often with the highest levels in the young
- Heart failure, cardiac contusion, post-arrest, sepsis, stroke and subarachnoid hemorrhage

## BNP and NT-proBNP

When a ventricle stretches, myocytes release B-type natriuretic peptide. It is a volume and pressure gauge, useful mainly for the dyspneic patient where heart failure and COPD look alike.

- **BNP:** under `100 pg/mL` makes acute heart failure unlikely; above `400 pg/mL` makes it likely.
- **NT-proBNP:** under `300 pg/mL` rules out acute heart failure. Rule-in cutoffs are age-adjusted: `450` under age `50`, `900` from `50` to `75`, `1,800` above `75`.

> **Trap:** Obesity lowers natriuretic peptides, so a heart failure patient with a BMI of `40` can present with a falsely reassuring BNP. Kidney failure, atrial fibrillation, and age raise it without any new heart failure. Sacubitril-valsartan raises BNP but not NT-proBNP.

## CK, CK-MB, and rhabdomyolysis

Creatine kinase (CK) runs `30-200 U/L` and rises with any muscle injury. CK-MB is the cardiac-enriched isoform; high-sensitivity troponin made it obsolete for diagnosing MI, and it survives mainly in some protocols for detecting reinfarction because it clears faster.

CK earns its keep in **rhabdomyolysis**. A CK above `5x` the upper limit, roughly `1,000 U/L`, defines it. Above `5,000 U/L` the risk of acute kidney injury climbs sharply, because myoglobin is toxic to tubules. Treatment is aggressive isotonic fluid targeting urine output of `200-300 mL/h`.

> **On shift:** A urine dipstick positive for blood with no red cells on microscopy is myoglobin, not bleeding. That combination is the bedside clue to rhabdomyolysis.

## The HEART score

For chest pain, the HEART score scores **H**istory, **E**CG, **A**ge, **R**isk factors, and **T**roponin from `0` to `2` each, for a total of `0-10`. A score of `0-3` is low risk with roughly `1.7%` major cardiac events at six weeks; `4-6` is moderate and earns observation; `7-10` is high risk.
keyPoints: hs-troponin uses sex-specific 99th percentile cutoffs and a 0/1-hour or 0/2-hour delta, not a single value
Troponin means myocardial injury; sepsis, PE, CKD, and myocarditis all raise it without plaque rupture
BNP under 100 or NT-proBNP under 300 argues against acute heart failure; obesity lowers it, kidney disease raises it
CK above 5,000 U/L in rhabdomyolysis means real AKI risk; fluids target 200-300 mL/h of urine
HEART score 0-3 is low risk with about 1.7% events at six weeks

checks.q: A septic patient with a heart rate of 140 has an hs-troponin of 90 ng/L that is 95 ng/L two hours later. What does this pattern suggest?
choices: Chronic or demand-related myocardial injury, not an acute plaque event
checks.why: An elevated but flat troponin means injury without an acute rise-and-fall. In sepsis with tachycardia this is type 2 demand ischemia or chronic elevation. Acute infarction produces a significant delta between draws.

checks.q: A 55-year-old with a BMI of 42 is short of breath. NT-proBNP is 280 pg/mL. What is the safest interpretation?
choices: Heart failure is less likely, but obesity lowers the value so clinical assessment still governs
The test is invalid in anyone over 50
checks.why: NT-proBNP under 300 has a high negative predictive value, but obesity systematically lowers natriuretic peptides, so a value near the cutoff in a patient with a BMI of 42 loses some of that reassurance. Age raises cutoffs; it does not invalidate the test.

checks.q: A patient found down for 12 hours has a CK of 46,000 U/L. Urine dips 3+ blood with no RBCs on microscopy. What is the priority?
choices: Aggressive isotonic IV fluids targeting 200-300 mL/h urine output
Start antibiotics for urinary tract infection
Give a diuretic to flush the kidneys
checks.why: Dipstick blood without red cells is myoglobin from rhabdomyolysis. Myoglobin is nephrotoxic, so early aggressive isotonic fluid to maintain high urine flow is the intervention that protects the kidney. Diuretics without volume repletion worsen the injury.

lessons.title: Coagulation, D-dimer, and the clot rules
lessons.body:
## Two tests, two halves of the same cascade

Clotting is a chain of enzymes that ends in fibrin. The lab splits it in half and times each half.

**Prothrombin time (PT)**, normal `11-13.5` seconds, tests the extrinsic and common pathways. Because different labs use different reagents, the PT is converted into the **INR** (international normalized ratio), normal `0.8-1.1`, so that a `2.5` in New Jersey means the same as a `2.5` in Berlin.

**Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT)**, normal `25-35` seconds, tests the intrinsic and common pathways.

## Which drug each one follows

Warfarin blocks vitamin K recycling, which shuts down factors `II, VII, IX, X` plus proteins C and S. Factor VII has the shortest half-life, about `6` hours, so the PT and INR move first, and that is why warfarin is monitored by INR.

- INR target `2.0-3.0` for atrial fibrillation and venous thromboembolism.
- INR target `2.5-3.5` for a mechanical mitral valve.
- Life-threatening bleeding on warfarin: vitamin K `10 mg IV` plus four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate.

Unfractionated heparin is monitored by aPTT, targeting roughly `1.5-2.5x` control, commonly `60-80` seconds. Low molecular weight heparin (enoxaparin) is dosed by weight and needs no routine monitoring; if you must check it, the test is an anti-Xa level. Direct oral anticoagulants such as apixaban and rivaroxaban are not reliably reflected by either PT or aPTT.

> **Trap:** A normal PT and aPTT do not mean the patient is not anticoagulated. Someone on apixaban can have perfectly normal coagulation studies and still bleed like they are anticoagulated, because they are.

## Fibrinogen and the DIC panel

Fibrinogen, normal `200-400 mg/dL`, is the raw material for clot. It is an acute phase reactant, so inflammation drives it up. It falls when clotting consumes it. A fibrinogen under `150-200 mg/dL` in postpartum hemorrhage is an ominous number and is replaced with cryoprecipitate.

Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is simultaneous clotting and bleeding. The panel shows a low platelet count, prolonged PT and aPTT, a low fibrinogen, and a very high D-dimer, with schistocytes on the smear.

## D-dimer: a very good "no" and a terrible "yes"

D-dimer is a fragment left over when plasmin chews up cross-linked fibrin. It rises any time a clot has formed and is being broken down anywhere in the body. Sensitivity for pulmonary embolism runs about `95-98%`, but specificity is only around `40%`. Pregnancy, surgery, trauma, cancer, infection, and simply being old all raise it.

> **Key:** D-dimer is only useful when pretest probability is already low or intermediate. Ordering it on a high-risk patient is a mistake: a negative will not reassure you, and you were going to scan anyway.

The usual cutoff is `500 ng/mL FEU`. Above age `50`, the **age-adjusted cutoff** is `age x 10`, so a `78`-year-old uses `780 ng/mL`. This raises specificity without measurably missing clots.

## The rules that stand in front of the test

**PERC** applies only to patients you already judged low risk. All eight must be negative to skip testing entirely: age under `50`, heart rate under `100`, room-air oxygen saturation `95%` or higher, no unilateral leg swelling, no hemoptysis, no surgery or trauma in `4` weeks, no prior venous thromboembolism, and no estrogen use.

**Wells for PE** scores: clinical signs of DVT `3`, PE the most likely diagnosis `3`, heart rate over `100` `1.5`, immobilization or surgery in `4` weeks `1.5`, previous PE or DVT `1.5`, hemoptysis `1`, malignancy `1`. Four or less means PE unlikely, so a D-dimer decides. Over four means go straight to CT pulmonary angiography.

**Wells for DVT** gives `1` point each for active cancer, paralysis or recent immobilization, bedridden more than `3` days or major surgery within `12` weeks, tenderness along the deep veins, whole-leg swelling, calf swelling more than `3 cm` larger than the other side, pitting edema, collateral superficial veins, and previous DVT, then subtracts `2` if another diagnosis is at least as likely. Two or more means DVT is likely, so go to compression ultrasound.
keyPoints: PT and INR follow warfarin; aPTT follows unfractionated heparin; DOACs follow neither
INR target 2.0-3.0 for AF and VTE, 2.5-3.5 for a mechanical mitral valve; reverse major bleeding with vitamin K 10 mg IV plus 4-factor PCC
DIC: low platelets, long PT and aPTT, low fibrinogen, very high D-dimer
D-dimer is sensitive and nonspecific, so it only helps in low or intermediate pretest probability; age-adjusted cutoff is age x 10 over age 50
PERC negative on all eight stops the workup; Wells over 4 for PE sends the patient straight to CTA

checks.q: A 72-year-old with pleuritic chest pain has a Wells score of 2 and a D-dimer of 640 ng/mL FEU. Using the age-adjusted cutoff, what happens next?
choices: The D-dimer is negative at a cutoff of 720, so no CT is needed
The D-dimer is positive because 640 exceeds 500, so CT is required
The age-adjusted cutoff does not apply under age 75
checks.why: The age-adjusted cutoff is age x 10, so 72 x 10 = 720 ng/mL. With Wells of 2 (PE unlikely) and a D-dimer of 640 below that cutoff, PE is excluded without imaging. Applying the flat 500 cutoff here would generate an unnecessary CT.

checks.q: A patient on apixaban arrives after a fall with a head strike. PT 12 s, INR 1.0, aPTT 30 s. What is the correct interpretation?
choices: The patient is not anticoagulated and can be cleared
Normal coagulation studies do not exclude DOAC effect; treat them as anticoagulated
The aPTT must be repeated with a different reagent
Vitamin K should be given to normalize the INR
checks.why: Apixaban and rivaroxaban do not reliably prolong PT or aPTT, so normal values are meaningless for DOAC effect. Anticoagulated head trauma warrants imaging and observation. Vitamin K does not reverse a factor Xa inhibitor.

checks.q: A septic patient has platelets 42,000, INR 2.1, aPTT 58 s, fibrinogen 90 mg/dL, D-dimer over 20,000. What is the diagnosis?
checks.why: Low platelets, both clotting times prolonged, a consumed fibrinogen, and a massive D-dimer is the DIC pattern. Warfarin and vitamin K deficiency prolong the PT with a normal fibrinogen and normal platelets. Hemophilia prolongs only the aPTT.

lessons.title: Blood gases and the four-step read
lessons.body:
## Arterial versus venous: what you actually lose

An arterial blood gas (ABG) is drawn from the radial artery into a heparinized syringe. It hurts, it takes skill, and it can cause a hematoma or spasm. A venous blood gas (VBG) comes off any ordinary venipuncture or an existing line.

Compared with an ABG, a VBG runs a pH about `0.03-0.05` lower, a bicarbonate within `1-2 mEq/L`, and a `PCO2` roughly `4-6 mmHg` higher and less predictable. Everything you need for acid-base is therefore in a VBG.

> **Key:** A VBG answers "what is the acid-base status?" An ABG is the only one that answers "how well is this lung putting oxygen into blood?", because only it gives a true `PaO2`.

Normal arterial values: pH `7.35-7.45`, `PaCO2 35-45 mmHg`, `PaO2 80-100 mmHg`, `HCO3 22-26 mEq/L`, base excess `-2 to +2`.

## The four steps

1. **Look at the pH.** Below `7.35` is acidemia, above `7.45` is alkalemia. If it is normal, you may still have two opposing disorders.
2. **Find the driver.** If the `PaCO2` moves in the direction that explains the pH, the problem is respiratory. If the `HCO3` does, it is metabolic. Carbon dioxide is acid, bicarbonate is base.
3. **Check compensation.** For metabolic acidosis use **Winter's formula**: expected `PaCO2 = 1.5 x HCO3 + 8`, plus or minus `2`. If the measured `PaCO2` is higher than expected, there is an added respiratory acidosis; lower, an added respiratory alkalosis. For acute respiratory acidosis, bicarbonate rises about `1 mEq/L` for every `10 mmHg` of `PaCO2` above `40`; chronically it rises about `3-4`.
4. **If it is a metabolic acidosis, calculate the anion gap.**

## Three worked examples

**Case A.** pH `7.21`, `PaCO2 24`, `HCO3 10`, Na `138`, Cl `100`. Acidemic. Bicarbonate is low, so metabolic acidosis. Winter's predicts `1.5 x 10 + 8 = 23`, plus or minus `2`, and the measured `24` fits, so respiratory compensation is appropriate. Gap is `138 - 110 = 28`, wide. This is a **compensated high anion gap metabolic acidosis** and the patient is in diabetic ketoacidosis.

**Case B.** pH `7.28`, `PaCO2 62`, `HCO3 28`. Acidemic with a high `PaCO2`, so respiratory acidosis. Acute compensation would predict a bicarbonate near `26`, and `28` is barely above it, so this is mostly acute, perhaps acute on chronic. A COPD exacerbation or an opioid overdose looks like this.

**Case C.** pH `7.50`, `PaCO2 28`, `HCO3 22`. Alkalemic with a low `PaCO2`: acute respiratory alkalosis from blowing off carbon dioxide. Early salicylate toxicity, pulmonary embolism, pain, sepsis, and anxiety all do this. Anxiety is a diagnosis of exclusion.

## The A-a gradient

The alveolar-arterial gradient asks whether oxygen is crossing the membrane. On room air the shortcut is:

`A-a gradient = 150 - (PaCO2 / 0.8) - PaO2`

Normal is roughly `(age / 4) + 4`. A **normal gradient with hypoxemia** means the alveoli are not being ventilated at all, that is, hypoventilation from opioids or fatigue. A **widened gradient** means gas is not crossing: pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary edema, ARDS.

## Pulse oximetry is not a blood gas

The oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve is S-shaped. `PaO2 60 mmHg` corresponds to `SpO2 90%`; `PaO2 40` to about `75%`. Above `60` the curve flattens, so an `SpO2` of `99%` and `94%` can hide a large difference in `PaO2`. Below `90%` the curve falls off a cliff and small drops in oxygen mean big drops in saturation.

> **Trap:** The pulse oximeter is fooled by carbon monoxide, which it reads as oxygenated hemoglobin and reports as a falsely normal number, and by methemoglobin, which pins the reading near `85%` regardless of the truth. Suspect these and send a co-oximetry panel.
keyPoints: A VBG is adequate for pH, bicarbonate and approximate CO2; only an ABG gives a true PaO2
Four steps: pH, driver, compensation, then the anion gap if it is a metabolic acidosis
Winter's formula: expected PaCO2 = 1.5 x HCO3 + 8, plus or minus 2
A normal A-a gradient with hypoxemia means hypoventilation; a wide gradient means a lung problem
SpO2 90% equals PaO2 60 mmHg; carbon monoxide reads falsely normal and methemoglobin pins near 85%

checks.q: pH 7.30, PaCO2 30 mmHg, HCO3 14 mEq/L, Na 140, Cl 104. What is the full interpretation?
choices: High anion gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation
Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with inadequate compensation
checks.why: Acidemic with a low bicarbonate means metabolic acidosis. Winter's predicts 1.5 x 14 + 8 = 29, and the measured 30 fits, so compensation is appropriate. The gap is 140 - (104 + 14) = 22, which is wide.

checks.q: A patient on 2 L nasal cannula reads SpO2 100% but is confused after being rescued from a house fire. What is the concern?
choices: The oximeter proves oxygenation is fine
Carboxyhemoglobin is read as oxyhemoglobin, so the saturation is falsely reassuring; send co-oximetry
checks.why: A standard pulse oximeter cannot distinguish carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin and reports a falsely normal saturation in carbon monoxide poisoning. Methemoglobin pins the reading near 85%, not 100%. Co-oximetry measures both directly.

checks.q: An opioid overdose has PaO2 55 mmHg, PaCO2 70 mmHg on room air. Is the A-a gradient wide?
choices: Yes, roughly 40, so the lung parenchyma is diseased
No, roughly 8, consistent with pure hypoventilation
The gradient cannot be calculated without an ABG from the femoral artery
Yes, and it proves pulmonary embolism
checks.why: 150 - (70 / 0.8) - 55 = 150 - 87.5 - 55, which is about 7.5. A normal gradient with hypoxemia means the alveoli are simply not being ventilated: the opioid is suppressing respiratory drive, and the lung itself is fine.

lessons.title: Urinalysis, pregnancy testing, and toxicology
lessons.body:
## The dipstick, pad by pad

Urine is filtered plasma, so it reports on the kidney, the bladder, and anything the body is dumping.

- **Specific gravity** `1.005-1.030`: concentration. High means dry, low means dilute or a kidney that cannot concentrate.
- **pH** `4.5-8.0`: persistently alkaline urine suggests a urea-splitting organism such as Proteus, which also forms struvite stones.
- **Leukocyte esterase:** an enzyme from white cells. Sensitive for pyuria, less specific.
- **Nitrite:** gram-negative bacteria convert dietary nitrate to nitrite, but it takes about `4` hours of bladder dwell. Very specific, poorly sensitive, and negative with Enterococcus and Staphylococcus, which do not make the enzyme.
- **Blood, protein, ketones, glucose:** glucose spills once serum exceeds roughly `180 mg/dL`.

Leukocyte esterase positive with nitrite positive in a symptomatic patient is a urinary tract infection. Nitrite negative does not clear anything.

## Microscopy separates infection from contamination

More than `5-10` white cells per high power field is pyuria. More than `3` red cells per high power field is hematuria. More than `5` **squamous epithelial cells** per low power field means skin flora got into the cup, and the whole specimen should be recollected as a clean catch or a straight catheter sample.

Casts are molds of the tubule and tell you the problem is in the kidney itself:

| Cast | Means |
|---|---|
| White cell casts | Pyelonephritis |
| Red cell casts | Glomerulonephritis |
| Muddy brown granular | Acute tubular necrosis |
| Hyaline | Normal, concentrated urine, exercise |

Crystals matter in two situations: envelope-shaped calcium oxalate in a suspected ethylene glycol ingestion, and coffin-lid struvite with Proteus infection.

> **Trap:** Dipstick blood with no red cells on microscopy is not bleeding. It is myoglobin from rhabdomyolysis or free hemoglobin from hemolysis.

## Pregnancy testing

Urine hCG turns positive around `20-25 mIU/mL`, roughly one week after implantation. Serum quantitative hCG detects down to `1-5 mIU/mL` and gives a number you can trend: in a normal early intrauterine pregnancy it roughly **doubles every 48 hours**.

The **discriminatory zone** is the serum hCG above which a normal intrauterine pregnancy should be visible on transvaginal ultrasound, commonly quoted near `3,500 mIU/mL`. An hCG above that with an empty uterus is an ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise.

> **On shift:** Any woman of childbearing age with abdominal pain, syncope, or shock gets a pregnancy test before imaging and before most medications. It is the cheapest test that changes the most decisions.

## The urine drug screen and what it cannot do

The standard screen is an immunoassay aimed at drug classes, not specific molecules, and it reports exposure over days, not impairment now.

Common false positives: pseudoephedrine and bupropion reading as amphetamine, sertraline and efavirenz as benzodiazepine, some quinolones and rifampin as opiate, dextromethorphan and ketamine as PCP.

Common false negatives matter more. The opiate assay is built around morphine and codeine. It frequently misses oxycodone and reliably misses methadone, buprenorphine, and **fentanyl**, which requires a separate dedicated assay. A negative screen in a suspected overdose excludes nothing.

## The levels worth knowing

- **Acetaminophen:** draw at `4` hours post-ingestion and plot on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram; the treatment line starts at `150 mcg/mL` at `4` hours. Treat with N-acetylcysteine.
- **Salicylate:** therapeutic `15-30 mg/dL`, toxic above `40-50`. The signature is a mixed respiratory alkalosis with a wide anion gap acidosis.
- **Digoxin:** therapeutic `0.5-2.0 ng/mL`. Toxicity brings nausea, yellow-green vision, bradyarrhythmias, and, in acute overdose, hyperkalemia. Antidote is digoxin immune Fab.
- **Lithium:** `0.6-1.2 mEq/L`; above `2.5` with symptoms is a dialysis conversation.
- **Phenytoin:** total `10-20 mcg/mL`, but it is protein bound, so check a free level when albumin is low.
- **Vancomycin trough:** `15-20 mcg/mL` for serious infection, drawn within `30` minutes before the fourth dose.
- **Ethanol:** the legal limit is `0.08 g/dL`, which is `80 mg/dL`. Serum levels run `12-20%` higher than whole blood, and a legal draw needs chain of custody and a non-alcohol skin prep.
- **Carboxyhemoglobin:** normal under `3%`, under `10%` in smokers, severe above `25%`. **Methemoglobin:** symptomatic above `15%`, treated with methylene blue `1-2 mg/kg`.
keyPoints: Leukocyte esterase plus nitrite in a symptomatic patient means UTI; nitrite is specific but insensitive
More than 5 squamous cells per low power field means contamination, so recollect
White cell casts mean pyelonephritis, red cell casts mean glomerulonephritis, muddy brown casts mean ATN
Serum hCG above roughly 3,500 mIU/mL with an empty uterus on transvaginal ultrasound means ectopic until proven otherwise
The urine drug screen misses fentanyl, methadone and buprenorphine entirely; fentanyl needs its own assay

checks.q: A urinalysis shows 20 WBC/hpf, many bacteria, and 15 squamous epithelial cells/lpf. What is the best next step?
choices: Recollect a clean catch or catheter specimen before deciding
Order a CT of the abdomen
Treat for a sexually transmitted infection
checks.why: Squamous epithelial cells come from skin and perineum, and more than 5 per low power field means the sample is contaminated. The white cells and bacteria may be from the skin, not the bladder, so the specimen must be recollected before it is acted on.

checks.q: A woman with a serum hCG of 4,200 mIU/mL has a transvaginal ultrasound showing an empty uterus. What does this mean?
choices: A normal pregnancy that is simply too early to see
The hCG must be a false positive
checks.why: Above the discriminatory zone of roughly 3,500 mIU/mL a normal intrauterine pregnancy should be visible on transvaginal ultrasound. An empty uterus above that level means ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise. A completed miscarriage would require prior documentation of an intrauterine pregnancy or a falling hCG.

checks.q: A patient found unresponsive with pinpoint pupils has a negative urine opiate screen. What follows?
choices: The screen misses fentanyl, methadone and buprenorphine, so opioid overdose is still very much on the table
The screen must be repeated in 24 hours
checks.why: Standard opiate immunoassays target morphine and codeine. Fentanyl, methadone and buprenorphine are structurally different and are not detected without dedicated assays. Clinical findings of pinpoint pupils and respiratory depression outrank a negative screen.

lessons.title: Lactate, cultures, spinal fluid, and the blood bank
lessons.body:
## Lactate is a perfusion alarm

When a cell cannot get enough oxygen to run aerobic metabolism, it ferments pyruvate to lactate instead. Serum lactate under `2.0 mmol/L` is normal, `2.0-4.0` is intermediate and worrying, and `4.0 mmol/L` or higher is the threshold that, with suspected infection, defines septic shock physiology and triggers the sepsis bundle: blood cultures, antibiotics within one hour, `30 mL/kg` of crystalloid, and a **repeat lactate within 2 to 4 hours**. Clearance of more than `10%` is the goal.

Not every lactate is shock. A generalized seizure produces a lactate of `5` or more that clears within an hour. Albuterol drives glycolysis directly. Metformin, liver failure, thiamine deficiency, and epinephrine infusions all raise it. Mesenteric ischemia raises it late, which is why a soft abdomen with pain out of proportion should scare you before the lactate does.

## Cultures and the clock

Blood cultures are two sets from two separate sites, drawn **before** antibiotics, with `10 mL` in each bottle for adults. Volume is the single biggest determinant of yield. Each set has an aerobic and an anaerobic bottle.

| Stage | Timing | What you get |
|---|---|---|
| Gram stain | `1 hour` | Shape and stain: gram-positive cocci in clusters |
| Growth signal | `12-48 hours` | Something is growing |
| Species and sensitivities | `24-72 hours` | The name and the antibiotic it dies to |

Contamination looks like one bottle of one set growing coagulase-negative Staphylococcus, Corynebacterium, or Cutibacterium after `3` or more days. True bacteremia grows fast and in multiple bottles.

Other specimens: a urine culture is significant at `100,000 CFU/mL` of a single organism, while mixed flora means contamination. A sputum sample is only a real lower-airway specimen if it has more than `25` neutrophils and fewer than `10` squamous cells per low power field. Wound swabs of the surface grow colonizers; deep tissue or aspirate is far better. A **MRSA nasal PCR** has a negative predictive value near `95-99%` for MRSA pneumonia, which is why a negative swab is used to stop vancomycin.

## Inflammation markers

CRP rises within `6` hours, peaks near `48`, and falls quickly, so it tracks change. ESR climbs over days and stays elevated for weeks, making it useful for osteomyelitis and temporal arteritis. Procalcitonin rises with bacterial infection and stays low in viral illness; its real use is deciding when to **stop** antibiotics, not whether to withhold them in someone who looks septic.

For pharyngitis, the **Centor** criteria give one point each for fever, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes, and absence of cough, adding one for age `3-14` and subtracting one at `45` or older. For pneumonia, **CURB-65** gives one point each for confusion, BUN above `19 mg/dL`, respiratory rate `30` or more, systolic BP under `90` or diastolic `60` or less, and age `65` or older; `0-1` can usually go home.

## Spinal fluid

Normal cerebrospinal fluid is clear, with an opening pressure of `10-20 cm H2O`, `0-5` white cells that are lymphocytes, protein `15-45 mg/dL`, and glucose `45-80 mg/dL`, about two-thirds of the serum value.

| Finding | Bacterial | Viral |
|---|---|---|
| Appearance | Cloudy | Clear |
| White cells | `1,000-5,000`, neutrophils | `10-500`, lymphocytes |
| Protein | Over `200 mg/dL` | Mildly raised |
| Glucose | Under `40`, low ratio | Normal |

**Xanthochromia** is a yellow tint in the spun supernatant from broken-down red cells. It takes `6-12` hours to develop and supports subarachnoid hemorrhage. A traumatic tap instead shows blood that clears from tube one to tube four.

## The blood bank

A **type and screen** determines ABO and Rh type and screens the patient's serum for unexpected antibodies. It takes roughly `45` minutes and is what you order when transfusion is possible but not certain. A **crossmatch** physically tests the chosen donor unit against the patient's serum and adds `15-30` minutes, though an electronic crossmatch is faster when the antibody screen is negative.

When there is no time, **emergency release O-negative** blood goes out uncrossmatched. O-negative is reserved for girls and women of childbearing potential to avoid Rh sensitization; O-positive is acceptable for males and older women.

> **Key:** The specimen label is the safety system. Two identifiers confirmed at the bedside, the tube labeled at the bedside before you leave it. A mislabeled blood bank tube is rejected without exception, because an ABO-incompatible transfusion can kill in minutes.
keyPoints: Lactate 4.0 mmol/L or more with suspected infection drives the sepsis bundle and a repeat lactate in 2-4 hours
Seizures, albuterol, metformin and liver disease raise lactate without shock
Two sets of blood cultures, 10 mL per bottle, before antibiotics; gram stain in an hour, sensitivities in 24-72 hours
Bacterial CSF: cloudy, neutrophils in the thousands, protein over 200, glucose under 40. Viral: clear, lymphocytes, normal glucose
Type and screen takes about 45 minutes; emergency O-negative is for women of childbearing potential, and bedside labeling is non-negotiable

checks.q: A patient who just had a generalized tonic-clonic seizure has a lactate of 6.2 mmol/L, normal blood pressure, and is waking up. What is the most reasonable action?
choices: Recognize post-ictal lactate and recheck in an hour while looking for a seizure cause
checks.why: A generalized seizure produces marked lactate from muscle activity that clears within about an hour. With normal perfusion and improving mentation, the number reflects the seizure, not shock. Chasing it with a sepsis bundle treats the lab instead of the patient.

checks.q: CSF shows 2,400 WBC with 90% neutrophils, protein 310 mg/dL, glucose 22 mg/dL with a serum glucose of 110. What is this?
checks.why: Neutrophil-predominant pleocytosis in the thousands, very high protein, and a glucose well under 40 and far below two-thirds of serum is the bacterial pattern. Viral meningitis gives hundreds of lymphocytes with a normal glucose. Subarachnoid hemorrhage gives red cells and xanthochromia.

checks.q: A 24-year-old woman in hemorrhagic shock needs blood now. What is released?
choices: O-positive, since it is more available
O-negative, to avoid Rh sensitization in a woman of childbearing potential
Wait 45 minutes for the type and screen
checks.why: Uncrossmatched emergency blood is type O. O-negative is prioritized for girls and women of childbearing potential because Rh sensitization threatens future pregnancies. AB-positive is the universal plasma donor and universal red cell recipient, not a universal red cell donor.

lessons.title: Imaging: the chest film, the CT, and the rules that say no
lessons.body:
## Read every chest X-ray the same way

A systematic read beats a talented eye, because a system cannot get distracted by the obvious finding and miss the second one. Use **ABCDE**.

- **A - Airway:** the trachea should be midline. A tension pneumothorax pushes it away; a collapsed lobe pulls it toward.
- **B - Bones and soft tissue:** ribs, clavicles, and subcutaneous air.
- **C - Cardiac silhouette:** on a proper PA film the heart should be less than `50%` of the chest width (the cardiothoracic ratio).
- **D - Diaphragm:** both domes smooth, right slightly higher because of the liver, and both costophrenic angles sharp. Blunting means effusion, which needs about `200-300 mL` to show on an upright film. Air under the diaphragm means a perforated viscus.
- **E - Everything else:** compare left lung to right, zone by zone.

The patterns you must name: **pneumonia** is a focal white consolidation with air bronchograms, located by the silhouette sign (a lost right heart border means right middle lobe). **Heart failure** is upper-lobe vessel redistribution, Kerley B lines, perihilar haze, bilateral effusions, and a big heart. **Pneumothorax** is a thin white pleural line with nothing but blackness beyond it. **COPD** is more than `10` posterior ribs of hyperinflation with flat diaphragms.

> **Trap:** A portable AP film magnifies the heart by up to `20%`, so you cannot diagnose cardiomegaly on one. Supine films also let effusions layer out as a vague haze instead of a meniscus.

Line checks: an endotracheal tube tip sits `3-5 cm` above the carina, a central line tip at the cavoatrial junction, and a nasogastric tube must cross the diaphragm with its side port past the stomach entrance.

## CT: the contrast question is the whole question

| Study | Contrast | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Head, stroke or trauma | **Without** | Fresh blood is already bright white; contrast would hide it |
| CTA head and neck | With | Large-vessel occlusion, dissection |
| CTA chest, PE protocol | With, timed | Contrast must be in the pulmonary arteries |
| Abdomen and pelvis | With IV | Appendicitis, obstruction, abscess |
| Renal colic protocol | Without | Stones are dense enough on their own |

Iodinated contrast cautions: a previous anaphylactoid reaction earns premedication with prednisone `50 mg` at `13`, `7`, and `1` hours before, plus diphenhydramine `50 mg`. Shellfish allergy is not a contraindication, which is a myth worth unlearning. For kidneys, check the eGFR; metformin itself is not harmed by contrast, but it is held for `48` hours after when the eGFR is under `30` or acute kidney injury develops, because metformin plus kidney failure causes lactic acidosis.

Dose awareness: a chest X-ray is about `0.1 mSv`, a head CT `2 mSv`, a chest CT `7 mSv`, and an abdomen and pelvis CT roughly `10 mSv`, against a natural background of about `3 mSv` per year.

## Ultrasound at the bedside

Ultrasound is free of radiation, portable, and answers yes-or-no questions in seconds. Free fluid is black.

- **FAST exam:** right upper quadrant, left upper quadrant, pelvis, and subxiphoid. Free fluid in a hypotensive trauma patient means the operating room.
- **Cardiac:** a pericardial effusion with the right ventricle collapsing in diastole is tamponade.
- **IVC:** a small, fully collapsing inferior vena cava suggests low volume.
- **Lung sliding present** excludes pneumothorax at that spot.
- **Compression ultrasound:** a vein that does not squash flat has clot in it.
- **First trimester:** transvaginal to find or fail to find an intrauterine pregnancy.

## MRI and plain films

MRI uses a powerful magnet, not radiation, and wins for soft tissue, spinal cord, and early stroke. The safety screen is the whole job: implanted metal, pacemakers and defibrillators, cochlear implants, aneurysm clips, and metal fragments in the eye, which is why welders get orbital X-rays first. Gadolinium is avoided or discussed carefully when the eGFR is under `30`.

Plain films need at least **two views at 90 degrees**, because a single view hides displacement, plus the joint above and below for a long bone. Weight-bearing views assess foot and ankle stability.

## Rules that tell you not to image

- **Ottawa ankle:** image only with malleolar pain plus bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of either malleolus, or inability to take `4` steps both immediately and in the department.
- **Ottawa knee:** age `55` or older, isolated patellar tenderness, fibular head tenderness, inability to flex to `90` degrees, or inability to take `4` steps.
- **Canadian CT head:** high risk is GCS under `15` at two hours, suspected open or depressed skull fracture, any sign of basilar skull fracture, two or more vomits, or age `65` or older.
- **NEXUS:** no imaging if all five are true - no midline cervical tenderness, no focal deficit, normal alertness, no intoxication, and no distracting injury.
keyPoints: ABCDE on every chest film: airway, bones, cardiac silhouette, diaphragm, everything else
Cardiomegaly cannot be called on a portable AP film because it magnifies the heart up to 20%
Head CT for bleed is WITHOUT contrast; PE and vascular studies are WITH timed contrast
Shellfish allergy is not a contrast contraindication; metformin is held 48 hours only with eGFR under 30 or AKI
Ottawa, Canadian CT head and NEXUS exist to justify not imaging, and each has explicit criteria

checks.q: A portable AP chest film on a supine patient shows a heart that looks enlarged. What can you conclude?
choices: Very little; AP portable technique magnifies the heart by up to 20%
The patient has a pericardial effusion
The film must be repeated with contrast
checks.why: On an AP film the heart sits farther from the detector and is magnified. Cardiothoracic ratio is only valid on an upright PA film taken at 6 feet. Effusion versus cardiomegaly is settled by echocardiography, not by a portable film, and chest X-rays do not use contrast.

checks.q: A 70-year-old on warfarin fell and struck his head. Which imaging study is correct first?
checks.why: Acute blood is hyperdense and obvious on a non-contrast head CT; adding contrast makes vessels bright and can obscure or mimic hemorrhage. MRI is slower and not the first study for acute bleed. Skull films do not show intracranial injury.

checks.q: A 30-year-old twisted her ankle, has no malleolar bone tenderness, and walked four steps in the department. What do the Ottawa ankle rules advise?
checks.why: The Ottawa ankle rules require malleolar zone pain plus bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of a malleolus, or inability to bear weight for four steps. With neither present the rule is negative and imaging can be safely skipped.

cards.front: What does a lab reference range actually represent?
cards.back: The middle 95% of results from a group the lab called healthy. By arithmetic alone, 1 in 20 healthy people falls outside any given range.

cards.front: What must happen when the lab reports a critical value?
cards.back: A technologist telephones a licensed provider, the provider repeats the value back, and the read-back is documented with the time and both names.

cards.front: Name five typical critical value thresholds.
cards.back: Potassium under 2.8 or over 6.2 mEq/L, sodium under 120 or over 160 mEq/L, glucose under 50 or over 450 mg/dL, platelets under 20,000, INR over 5.0.

cards.front: What is a delta check, and what should a wild delta make you suspect first?
cards.back: It compares a result to that patient's own prior value. A number that does not fit the patient is a specimen problem, wrong tube or wrong patient, until a redraw proves otherwise.

cards.front: A specimen is flagged hemolyzed. Which results become unreliable, and in which direction?
cards.back: Potassium, AST, and LDH are falsely high because red cells spilled their contents into the serum. Hemolysis is the number one cause of fake hyperkalemia.

cards.front: Explain SnNout and SpPin in one line each.
cards.back: SnNout: a highly sensitive test, when negative, rules the disease out. SpPin: a highly specific test, when positive, rules the disease in.

cards.front: How do you calculate the absolute neutrophil count (ANC)?
cards.back: ANC = WBC x (percent segs + percent bands) / 100. A WBC of 2,000 with 30% segs and 5% bands gives 2,000 x 0.35 = 700.

cards.front: Which ANC values define neutropenia, and which one is an emergency?
cards.back: Under 1,500 is neutropenia, under 1,000 moderate, under 500 severe. Fever with an ANC under 500 is febrile neutropenia: cultures then antibiotics within 60 minutes.

cards.front: What is a left shift, and why does a normal total WBC not reassure you?
cards.back: Immature neutrophils called bands released early because mature ones are being consumed. Bands over 10% suggests serious bacterial infection and can occur with a completely normal WBC.

cards.front: List the five white cell types with their normal percentages.
cards.back: Neutrophils 40-70%, lymphocytes 20-40%, monocytes 2-8%, eosinophils 1-4%, basophils 0-1%.

cards.front: What is the rule of 3 for hemoglobin and hematocrit?
cards.back: Hematocrit runs about three times the hemoglobin. Hgb 10 g/dL means Hct near 30%. If the two do not track, question the specimen.

cards.front: What are the two red cell transfusion thresholds, and how much does one unit raise the hemoglobin?
cards.back: 7 g/dL for most stable hospitalized patients; 8 g/dL for cardiac surgery, active coronary syndrome, and hip or knee surgery. One unit raises Hgb about 1 g/dL and Hct about 3%.

cards.front: How does the MCV sort anemia into causes?
cards.back: Under 80 fL: iron deficiency, thalassemia, chronic disease, lead. 80-100: blood loss, hemolysis, kidney disease. Over 100: B12 or folate deficiency, alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism.

cards.front: Why is a normal hemoglobin useless 20 minutes into a hemorrhage?
cards.back: Whole blood loss removes plasma and cells in the same ratio, so concentration is unchanged until fluid shifts in or crystalloid is given. Vitals, exam, and FAST decide, not the Hgb.

cards.front: Name the three platelet thresholds that change management.
cards.back: Under 50,000 cancel procedures and expect bleeding with trauma. Under 20,000 transfuse if febrile or bleeding. Under 10,000 transfuse prophylactically for spontaneous bleeding risk.

cards.front: Write the anion gap formula and its normal range.
cards.back: Anion gap = Na - (Cl + HCO3), normal 8-12 mEq/L. It widens when an unmeasured acid consumes bicarbonate and leaves its own anion behind.

cards.front: What does MUDPILES stand for?
cards.back: Methanol, Uremia, Diabetic ketoacidosis, Propylene glycol, Iron or Isoniazid, Lactate, Ethylene glycol, Salicylates. The causes of a wide anion gap metabolic acidosis.

cards.front: What does a BUN to creatinine ratio above 20:1 tell you?
cards.back: Pre-renal physiology. The kidney is reabsorbing urea along with sodium and water: dehydration, hemorrhage, heart failure, or a gastrointestinal bleed feeding protein into the gut.

cards.front: How do you correct calcium for a low albumin?
cards.back: Corrected calcium = measured calcium + 0.8 x (4.0 - albumin). Half of calcium rides on albumin, so a low albumin makes the total look low while ionized calcium is fine.

cards.front: In what order do you treat hyperkalemia, and what does each step do?
cards.back: Calcium gluconate 1 g IV stabilizes the membrane but does not lower potassium. Insulin 10 units with 25 g dextrose plus albuterol shifts it into cells. Then remove it.

cards.front: How fast may you correct a sodium of 118 mEq/L, and why does the limit exist?
cards.back: No more than about 8 mEq/L in 24 hours. Faster correction pulls water out of brain cells and causes osmotic demyelination. Seizures justify 3% saline, roughly 100 mL over 10 minutes.

cards.front: What are the HbA1c thresholds, and what does TSH plus free T4 pattern mean?
cards.back: HbA1c 5.7-6.4% is prediabetes, 6.5% or higher is diabetes. High TSH with low free T4 is primary hypothyroidism; low TSH with high free T4 is hyperthyroidism.

cards.front: What distinguishes a hepatocellular from a cholestatic liver pattern?
cards.back: Hepatocellular: AST and ALT rise far out of proportion to alkaline phosphatase. Cholestatic: alkaline phosphatase and direct bilirubin lead, with only modest transaminase rise.

cards.front: An AST to ALT ratio above 2:1 with both under 300 U/L means what?
cards.back: Alcoholic liver injury. Remember it as you toAST with alcohol. Viral hepatitis and fatty liver run ALT above AST, usually in the hundreds.

cards.front: Which three causes send transaminases above 1,000 U/L?
cards.back: Acetaminophen toxicity, ischemic hepatitis (shock liver), and acute viral hepatitis. Acetaminophen shows a near-normal early bilirubin with a rising INR.

cards.front: What is the shock liver signature?
cards.back: A transaminase spike into the thousands within 24 hours of hypotension, an LDH that rises alongside it, then a rapid fall over days once perfusion returns.

cards.front: Indirect versus direct bilirubin: what does each point to?
cards.back: Indirect (unconjugated) high: hemolysis or Gilbert syndrome, meaning too much heme or lazy conjugation. Direct (conjugated) high: obstruction, stones, strictures, tumors, and it darkens the urine.

cards.front: Alkaline phosphatase is high but GGT is normal. Where is it coming from?
cards.back: Bone, not liver. Think Paget disease, metastases, a healing fracture, or normal adolescent growth. A high GGT alongside would point to liver or bile duct.

cards.front: Which test reflects acute liver synthetic failure, and which reflects chronic?
cards.back: INR is acute, because clotting factors have half-lives of hours. Albumin is chronic, with a half-life near 20 days, so it stays normal in acute hepatitis.

cards.front: What is the lipase rule for pancreatitis, and does the height predict severity?
cards.back: Lipase at or above 3 times the upper limit with typical epigastric pain radiating to the back diagnoses pancreatitis. The height does not predict severity; vitals, calcium, BUN, and organ failures do.

cards.front: How is high-sensitivity troponin interpreted?
cards.back: Against a sex-specific 99th percentile, roughly 34 ng/L for men and 16 ng/L for women on a typical assay, and by the delta between a 0 and 1 or 0 and 2 hour draw, not a single value.

cards.front: What is the difference between a type 1 and a type 2 myocardial infarction?
cards.back: Type 1 is plaque rupture with thrombus. Type 2 is supply and demand mismatch with no plaque event: sepsis, tachyarrhythmia, severe anemia, hypotension, hypertensive crisis.

cards.front: Name four non-ACS causes of an elevated troponin.
cards.back: Pulmonary embolism through right ventricular strain, chronic kidney disease through reduced clearance, myocarditis, and heart failure. Also sepsis, cardiac contusion, and post-arrest.

cards.front: Give the BNP and NT-proBNP cutoffs for acute heart failure.
cards.back: BNP under 100 pg/mL makes it unlikely, over 400 likely. NT-proBNP under 300 rules out; rule-in is age-adjusted at 450 under 50, 900 from 50-75, and 1,800 over 75.

cards.front: Which conditions falsely lower and falsely raise natriuretic peptides?
cards.back: Obesity lowers BNP and NT-proBNP, which is falsely reassuring. Kidney failure, atrial fibrillation, and age raise them. Sacubitril-valsartan raises BNP but not NT-proBNP.

cards.front: What CK values define rhabdomyolysis and high kidney risk, and what is the treatment target?
cards.back: Above 5 times the upper limit, roughly 1,000 U/L, defines it. Above 5,000 U/L carries real AKI risk. Give aggressive isotonic fluid targeting 200-300 mL/h of urine.

cards.front: Urine dipstick is 3+ blood but microscopy shows no red cells. What is it?
cards.back: Myoglobin from rhabdomyolysis, or free hemoglobin from hemolysis. The dipstick detects heme, not intact cells, so this combination is the bedside clue to rhabdomyolysis.

cards.front: What does the HEART score include and what does a low score mean?
cards.back: History, ECG, Age, Risk factors, Troponin, scored 0-2 each for a total of 0-10. A score of 0-3 is low risk with about 1.7% major cardiac events at six weeks.

cards.front: Which pathway does PT and INR test, and which does aPTT test?
cards.back: PT and INR test the extrinsic and common pathways and follow warfarin. aPTT tests the intrinsic and common pathways and follows unfractionated heparin. Normal PT 11-13.5 s, aPTT 25-35 s.

cards.front: Which factors does warfarin block, and which moves the INR first?
cards.back: Factors II, VII, IX, X plus proteins C and S. Factor VII has the shortest half-life at about 6 hours, so the PT and INR move first.

cards.front: Give the INR targets and the reversal for life-threatening bleeding on warfarin.
cards.back: 2.0-3.0 for atrial fibrillation and venous thromboembolism, 2.5-3.5 for a mechanical mitral valve. Reverse with vitamin K 10 mg IV plus four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate.

cards.front: Why do normal PT and aPTT fail to exclude anticoagulation?
cards.back: Direct oral anticoagulants such as apixaban and rivaroxaban are not reliably reflected by either test. A patient on a DOAC can have normal studies and still be fully anticoagulated.

cards.front: What does the DIC panel show?
cards.back: Low platelets, prolonged PT and aPTT, a low fibrinogen from consumption, and a very high D-dimer, with schistocytes on the smear.

cards.front: What are D-dimer's sensitivity and specificity, and when is it useful?
cards.back: About 95-98% sensitive but only about 40% specific for PE. It is only useful at low or intermediate pretest probability, where a negative safely rules out.

cards.front: What is the age-adjusted D-dimer cutoff?
cards.back: Over age 50, the cutoff is age x 10 ng/mL FEU instead of the flat 500. A 78-year-old uses 780. It raises specificity without measurably missing clots.

cards.front: List the eight PERC criteria.
cards.back: Age under 50, heart rate under 100, room-air SpO2 at least 95%, no unilateral leg swelling, no hemoptysis, no surgery or trauma in 4 weeks, no prior VTE, no estrogen use. All eight negative in a low-risk patient stops the workup.

cards.front: What does a VBG give you reliably, and what does it not?
cards.back: Reliable pH (about 0.03-0.05 lower than arterial), bicarbonate within 1-2 mEq/L, and an approximate CO2 about 4-6 mmHg higher. It cannot give a true PaO2, so it never answers oxygenation.

cards.front: What are the four steps of an ABG read?
cards.back: 1. Look at the pH. 2. Find the driver, CO2 for respiratory or bicarbonate for metabolic. 3. Check whether compensation is appropriate. 4. If it is a metabolic acidosis, calculate the anion gap.

cards.front: State Winter's formula and what deviations mean.
cards.back: Expected PaCO2 = 1.5 x HCO3 + 8, plus or minus 2. A measured CO2 higher than expected adds a respiratory acidosis; lower adds a respiratory alkalosis.

cards.front: Give the room-air A-a gradient shortcut and the normal value.
cards.back: A-a gradient = 150 - (PaCO2 / 0.8) - PaO2. Normal is roughly (age / 4) + 4.

cards.front: Hypoxemia with a normal A-a gradient versus a wide one: what does each mean?
cards.back: Normal gradient means hypoventilation, as in opioids, sedation, or fatigue. Wide gradient means gas is not crossing: pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary edema, ARDS.

cards.front: Match SpO2 to PaO2 at the key points on the dissociation curve.
cards.back: SpO2 90% equals PaO2 about 60 mmHg. SpO2 75% equals PaO2 about 40 mmHg. Above 60 the curve flattens; below 90% it falls off a cliff.

cards.front: How do carbon monoxide and methemoglobin fool a pulse oximeter?
cards.back: Carboxyhemoglobin is read as oxyhemoglobin, giving a falsely normal or high saturation. Methemoglobin pins the reading near 85% regardless of the truth. Co-oximetry measures both directly.

cards.front: Why is a negative urine nitrite unhelpful?
cards.back: Nitrite is specific but insensitive. It requires gram-negative bacteria and about 4 hours of bladder dwell, and Enterococcus and Staphylococcus never produce it.

cards.front: What finding on microscopy means the urine specimen is contaminated?
cards.back: More than 5 squamous epithelial cells per low power field. Those come from skin and perineum, so the sample should be recollected as a clean catch or catheter specimen.

cards.front: What does each urinary cast type mean?
cards.back: White cell casts: pyelonephritis. Red cell casts: glomerulonephritis. Muddy brown granular casts: acute tubular necrosis. Hyaline casts: normal, concentrated urine, or exercise.

cards.front: What is the discriminatory zone, and how does hCG behave in a normal early pregnancy?
cards.back: Above a serum hCG near 3,500 mIU/mL a normal intrauterine pregnancy should be visible on transvaginal ultrasound; an empty uterus means ectopic until proven otherwise. Normally hCG roughly doubles every 48 hours.

cards.front: Which drugs cause common urine drug screen false positives?
cards.back: Pseudoephedrine and bupropion read as amphetamine, sertraline and efavirenz as benzodiazepine, some quinolones and rifampin as opiate, dextromethorphan and ketamine as PCP.

cards.front: Which opioids does the standard urine screen miss, and why?
cards.back: The assay targets morphine and codeine. It frequently misses oxycodone and reliably misses methadone, buprenorphine, and fentanyl. Fentanyl needs a separate dedicated assay.

cards.front: Compare the acetaminophen and salicylate workups.
cards.back: Acetaminophen: draw at 4 hours, plot on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram whose line starts at 150 mcg/mL, treat with N-acetylcysteine. Salicylate: toxic above 40-50 mg/dL, with a mixed respiratory alkalosis plus wide anion gap acidosis.

cards.front: Give the therapeutic ranges for digoxin, lithium, phenytoin, and a vancomycin trough.
cards.back: Digoxin 0.5-2.0 ng/mL, lithium 0.6-1.2 mEq/L, phenytoin total 10-20 mcg/mL (check a free level if albumin is low), vancomycin trough 15-20 mcg/mL for serious infection.

cards.front: What are the lactate thresholds and what does 4.0 mmol/L trigger?
cards.back: Under 2.0 is normal, 2.0-4.0 intermediate, 4.0 or above is severe. With suspected infection it triggers cultures, antibiotics within an hour, 30 mL/kg crystalloid, and a repeat lactate in 2-4 hours.

cards.front: Name five causes of a high lactate that are not shock.
cards.back: Generalized seizure (clears within an hour), albuterol, metformin, liver failure with impaired clearance, thiamine deficiency, and epinephrine infusions.

cards.front: How are blood cultures drawn, and what determines yield most?
cards.back: Two sets from two separate sites before antibiotics, aerobic and anaerobic bottles, 10 mL per bottle in adults. Volume of blood is the single biggest determinant of yield.

cards.front: What is the blood culture timeline, and what pattern means contamination?
cards.back: Gram stain about 1 hour, growth signal 12-48 hours, sensitivities 24-72 hours. Contamination is one bottle of one set growing coagulase-negative Staphylococcus or Cutibacterium after 3 days; true bacteremia grows fast in multiple bottles.

cards.front: How do CRP, ESR, and procalcitonin differ in use?
cards.back: CRP rises in 6 hours and falls fast, tracking change. ESR climbs over days and stays up for weeks, useful for osteomyelitis and temporal arteritis. Procalcitonin favors bacterial over viral and is used to stop antibiotics.

cards.front: Contrast bacterial and viral CSF findings.
cards.back: Bacterial: cloudy, 1,000-5,000 neutrophils, protein over 200 mg/dL, glucose under 40. Viral: clear, 10-500 lymphocytes, mildly raised protein, normal glucose. Normal CSF glucose is about two-thirds of serum.

cards.front: How do you tell subarachnoid hemorrhage from a traumatic tap?
cards.back: Xanthochromia, a yellow tint in the spun supernatant from broken-down red cells, takes 6-12 hours and supports SAH. A traumatic tap shows blood that clears from tube one to tube four.

cards.front: Type and screen, crossmatch, emergency release: what is each and how long?
cards.back: Type and screen is ABO, Rh and an antibody screen, about 45 minutes. Crossmatch tests the donor unit against patient serum, adding 15-30 minutes. Emergency release is uncrossmatched O-negative for women of childbearing potential, O-positive otherwise.

cards.front: What is the ABCDE chest X-ray read?
cards.back: Airway (trachea midline), Bones and soft tissue, Cardiac silhouette and cardiothoracic ratio, Diaphragm and costophrenic angles, Everything else comparing lung to lung.

cards.front: How much pleural fluid is needed to blunt a costophrenic angle, and what does air under the diaphragm mean?
cards.back: About 200-300 mL on an upright film blunts the angle. Free air under the diaphragm means a perforated hollow viscus.

cards.front: List the chest film findings of heart failure.
cards.back: Upper-lobe vessel redistribution (cephalization), Kerley B lines, perihilar haze, bilateral pleural effusions, and an enlarged cardiac silhouette.

cards.front: Why can you not diagnose cardiomegaly on a portable AP film?
cards.back: AP technique puts the heart farther from the detector and magnifies it by up to 20%. The cardiothoracic ratio under 50% is only valid on an upright PA film.

cards.front: Where should an endotracheal tube, a central line, and a nasogastric tube sit on film?
cards.back: Endotracheal tube tip 3-5 cm above the carina, central line tip at the cavoatrial junction, nasogastric tube across the diaphragm with the side port past the stomach entrance.

cards.front: Which CT studies use contrast and which do not?
cards.back: Without: head for bleed or stroke, and renal colic protocol. With: CTA head and neck, CTA chest for PE, and abdomen and pelvis for appendicitis, obstruction, or abscess.

cards.front: What are the real contrast cautions, and which one is a myth?
cards.back: Premedicate a prior anaphylactoid reaction with prednisone 50 mg at 13, 7, and 1 hours plus diphenhydramine 50 mg. Hold metformin 48 hours if eGFR is under 30 or AKI develops. Shellfish allergy is a myth.

cards.front: Give approximate radiation doses for common studies.
cards.back: Chest X-ray about 0.1 mSv, head CT about 2 mSv, chest CT about 7 mSv, abdomen and pelvis CT about 10 mSv, against a natural background of about 3 mSv per year.

cards.front: Name the four FAST exam windows and what a positive means.
cards.back: Right upper quadrant, left upper quadrant, pelvis, and subxiphoid pericardium. Black free fluid in a hypotensive trauma patient means the operating room. A negative FAST does not exclude injury.

cards.front: What are the NEXUS criteria?
cards.back: No cervical imaging if all five are true: no midline cervical tenderness, no focal neurologic deficit, normal alertness, no intoxication, and no distracting injury.

cards.front: State the Ottawa ankle rule.
cards.back: Image only with malleolar zone pain plus bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of either malleolus, or inability to take 4 steps both at the time of injury and in the department.
